title: War as Peace
subtitle: Seeing social force as Einstein saw physical force

blocks.html: Standing still, we used to feel the forces of our bodies and the Earth oppose each other. Falling was acceleration. When we threw rocks and when we fired cannonballs, they did not fly straight—they curved toward the ground.

Today, we are aware (on some level) that our intuitive picture is just a convenience. Looking through the window of relativity, falling is stillness; standing on the ground is accelerating upward; projectiles do fly straight, and, while they fly, space flows—from our “timelike” point of view.

That is the kind of move I am trying to make with social theory, where the single most important question now facing political scientists, economists, and psychologists, and the rest of us is whether to seek an end to all war. Is war a permanent feature of human life? Is world peace possible? Desirable? Is warfare itself evil?

Every question of ethics and policy depends on the foregoing articulations or aspects of that one question. War is our primordial background—our prehistory, our history, and our present. Other people and the rest of Nature try to take the food out of our mouths and, eventually, our own bodies turn on us. War is the shadow that conceives the coercive power of the state, the malleable monetary value of time, the masses of dangerous and damaged personalities.
If war could one day be forgotten, then we could finally hope to live in a world of choice and diversity, honest leaders, voluntary trade, and sound minds. Surely that should be our common hope?

I want to put forward some evidence and a theoretical movement for social theory to parallel the physical theory of general relativity. I do not think an end to all war should be our common hope; war is here to stay. To my surprise, and as with relativity, it is a happy thought.

The persistence of war waged by combatants that possess but do not use nuclear weapons against their enemies should function as a kind of proof that war cannot be ended. Any means powerful enough to end all war, like a nuclear deterrent, is too powerful to actually be used in armed conflict because the entity using it would be committing a crime against humanity and taking a big risk that it will lose its right or mandate to wage war.

The idea is not that human beings should always be at war; rather, the idea is that we are always at war; and we should attend to it. Although I expect the citation would irritate some Christians, I credit this inversion move to Jesus while acknowledging that Socrates walked so Jesus could run.
